title: Supply concentration, export restrictions and declining investment put critical mineral security at risk
key_claim: The 2026 Global Critical Minerals Outlook finds critical-minerals investment fell 9% in 2025; new US projects and Malaysian output cut the top rare-earth refiner's share from over 90% in 2023 to 85% in 2025, projected to fall to 70% by 2035; and an estimated $6.5 trillion in annual downstream production outside China could be jeopardised if the October 2025 controls are enacted fully.
frame_summary: The IEA argues that supply concentration, export restrictions and falling investment have turned critical-mineral concentration from a theoretical vulnerability into an immediate economic-security challenge, while targeted policy and investment in rare earths show diversification is possible but slow.
signals_supported: China rare-earth and magnet export controls escalate
verbatim_quote: In rare earth refining, new projects in the United States and production increases in Malaysia reduced the share of the top supplier from over 90% in 2023 to 85% in 2025, and if planned projects come online as scheduled, it is projected to fall to 70% by 2035.
verbatim_list: an estimated $6.5 trillion in annual downstream production outside China could be jeopardised if the measures are enacted fully

title: Global trade update (June 2026): The shifting dynamics of critical minerals trade
key_claim: Since 2020 nearly 100 new export measures (37 licensing requirements, 31 export taxes, 29 export bans, one quota) have been introduced on critical energy transition minerals; in 2025 the DRC accounted for 74% of cobalt mine output, Indonesia 67% of nickel and China 69% of rare-earth mine production; and 73 critical-mineral partnership agreements have been logged, 58 of them since 2022.
frame_summary: UNCTAD argues that surging demand meets highly concentrated supply and that governments are increasingly using export measures and partnership deals to secure access, risking a fragmentation of critical-minerals trade into competing blocs unless international cooperation strengthens.
signals_supported: G7 standards-based markets and allied buyers' club
verbatim_quote: Since 2020, nearly 100 new export measures have been introduced on critical energy transition minerals. These include 37 licensing requirements, 31 export taxes, 29 export bans and one export quota.

publisher: Ministry of Commerce of the People's Republic of China (MOFCOM)
title: MOFCOM Announcement No. 26 of 2026 on further improving the reporting and handling of violations of strategic mineral dual-use export controls
key_claim: MOFCOM Announcement No. 26, effective 1 July 2026, establishes a public reporting mechanism under which any organisation or individual may report suspected violations of strategic-mineral dual-use export controls, covering thirteen categories including unlicensed export, disguising controlled items by disassembly, third-country transshipment, and accepting foreign-government verification requests without authorisation.
frame_summary: MOFCOM frames the announcement as mobilising whole-of-society supervision to enforce its strategic-mineral export-control regime, extending enforcement from customs border checks to a networked reporting system across the supply chain.
verbatim_quote: 本公告自2026年7月1日起正式实施。

title: Securing America's Defense Supply Chains and Ensuring Domestic Acquisition of Critical Materials
key_claim: The 20 July 2026 executive order directs that from 1 January 2027 the Secretary of War and military departments cease issuing waivers under 10 U.S.C. 4872(c)(1) for acquiring covered materials except under an accepted mitigation plan, and requires prime contractors to map indentured bills of materials for national-security acquisitions and replace unreliable foreign suppliers.
frame_summary: The White House argues that securing the defence industrial base against economic subversion requires strict enforcement of domestic and allied sourcing rules, closing the waiver route that let contractors keep buying critical materials from adversary suppliers.
verbatim_quote: On January 1, 2027, the Secretary of War (Secretary) and the Secretaries of the military departments shall cease to issue waivers under 10 U.S.C. 4872(c)(1) for the acquisition of covered materials under 10 U.S.C. 4872, except as provided in subsection (b) of this section.

title: Raw materials: Council adopts position to reinforce the security of supply and the circularity of EU industry
date_evidence: Council of the EU Press release 4 March 2026 10:55
key_claim: On 4 March 2026 the Council adopted its negotiating position on amending the Critical Raw Materials Act, transferring identification of large critical-raw-material users to the Commission; the CRMA sets 2030 targets of 10% extraction, 40% processing and 25% recycling of strategic raw materials, and follows the December 2025 RESourceEU action plan.
frame_summary: The Council frames the CRMA amendment as strengthening EU security of supply and circularity by giving the Commission power to identify vulnerable large companies and propose risk-mitigation measures, responding to Chinese export restrictions on rare earths.
verbatim_quote: It sets 2030 targets for 10% extraction, 40% processing, and 25% recycling of strategic raw materials in the EU to reduce reliance on single-country suppliers.

publisher: Center for Strategic and International Studies
title: Rare Earth Export Restrictions One Year Later
key_claim: CSIS finds the Trump administration has committed over $7.3 billion across five US departments and agencies to rare-earth capacity, including a $110/kg price floor and offtake for MP Materials, but that displacement measured in actual output remains modest, US rare-earth imports never recovered to pre-restriction levels, and true resilience is a matter of execution over years.
frame_summary: CSIS argues the US response has been unprecedented in ambition but that the central challenge is now execution: distance travelled in financing and announcements has not yet produced displacement in metric tons, and supply chains remain exposed to Chinese leverage.
signals_supported: US government equity stakes and price floors
China rare-earth and magnet export controls escalate

title: China's Global Exports of Rare Earths: June 2026 Update
date_evidence: Published by: Silverado Policy Accelerator • Jun 26, 2026
key_claim: China's shipments of export-controlled rare-earth compounds and metals to the United States, which had briefly recovered in March and April 2026, fell to zero in May, the first time since September 2025; Japan continues to receive few compounds and metals after China's January 2026 limits, and global yttrium, terbium and lutetium exports remained constrained.
frame_summary: Silverado argues that China's rare-earth exports are increasingly shaped by political discretion rather than demand, with U.S.- and Japan-bound flows of controlled compounds throttled even as the formal truce holds.
signals_supported: China rare-earth and magnet export controls escalate
verbatim_quote: China’s shipments of export-controlled rare earth compounds and metals to the United States—which had briefly recovered in March and April—fell to zero in May.

title: Why One-Off Federal Investments Won't Make or Break US Critical Mineral Supply
key_claim: RFF argues recent federal equity stakes, loans and a price floor lack a clear prioritisation framework, that only the MP Materials deal matched urgency with scale, and that without action on prices and durable demand, government ownership alone will not shift the economics of a domestic industry in secular decline.
frame_summary: RFF argues that one-off federal investments and equity stakes cannot by themselves make US critical-mineral production competitive with China, because they do not address the underlying price and demand economics that determine whether projects are viable.
signals_supported: US government equity stakes and price floors

title: Recent China Export Control Actions Signal Active Enforcement for Rare Earths and Strategic Minerals
key_claim: Recent actions signal active Chinese enforcement: Japanese nationals were detained in Dalian in May 2026 over alleged rare-earth-related smuggling, a Chinese optics firm's chairman faced compulsory measures over germanium mislabelling, and MOFCOM Announcement No. 26 (effective 1 July) formalises a public reporting mechanism, while June's listing of MP Materials and USA Rare Earths carries extraterritorial reach.
frame_summary: Morgan Lewis argues China is moving from rule-setting to visible, active enforcement of its strategic-mineral export controls, with detentions, domestic prosecutions and a public reporting mechanism that materially raise compliance exposure for multinationals in any jurisdiction.
verbatim_quote: On June 24, 2026, MOFCOM published Announcement No. 26 of 2026, which formalizes the reporting and handling of violations involving strategic mineral dual-use export controls.

title: G7 aims to see China supply no more than 60% of rare earths
key_claim: At the June 2026 Evian summit, G7 leaders agreed that no single country should supply more than 60% of their rare-earth and permanent-magnet imports by 2030, with a longer-term aim of 50%, and promised specific targets for other critical minerals by end-2026, while officials conceded the 2030 goal is ambitious and may need quotas in sectors like defence.
frame_summary: The report frames the G7's 60% target as a genuine political commitment to diversify away from China but one whose delivery is doubtful given project delays, funding constraints and the scale of China's refining lead.
signals_supported: G7 standards-based markets and allied buyers' club
verbatim_quote: The Group of Seven countries have agreed that no single country should supply more than 60% of their imports of rare earths by 2030 in an effort to reduce their reliance on China.

title: INSIGHT: Trump's critical minerals pricing plan faces skeptical G7, divided industry
key_claim: The US push to underpin Western minerals production with price floors set by a Pentagon AI model faces skeptical G7 allies and a divided industry: European officials oppose US pricing sway, Washington favours fast bilateral deals over France's multilateral secretariat, and a first binding agreement could cover five to ten minerals including heavy rare earths, antimony, graphite and tungsten.
frame_summary: The report frames the US price-floor and trading-bloc plan as stumbling over cost, governance and transatlantic disagreement, casting doubt on whether the allied response can cohere into a workable alternative pricing system.
signals_supported: G7 standards-based markets and allied buyers' club
US government equity stakes and price floors
verbatim_quote: The first binding agreement could extend to five to 10 minerals, the sources said.

title: US army bases to host critical minerals plants in onshoring push
key_claim: The US Army will let REalloys, Titan Mining, ioneer and EnergyX build rare-earth, graphite, lithium and boron processing plants on military bases; the same week the Office of Strategic Capital extended a $725 million loan to Energy Fuels and $500 million to Phoenix Tailings, on top of USA Rare Earth's $1.6 billion January package and a February plan for a $12 billion critical-minerals stockpile.
frame_summary: The report frames on-base processing as a first-of-its-kind extension of the US industrial-policy toolkit, using military property to accelerate domestic capacity as geopolitical tension over minerals shows no sign of easing.
verbatim_quote: The federal government also unveiled plans in February to build a $12 billion stockpile of critical minerals.

title: Op-Ed: DRC is setting the terms of global competition for critical minerals
key_claim: The DRC, which accounts for roughly 80% of global cobalt production, has used a quota system to lift cobalt prices from about $21,000 per tonne in early 2025 to just over $56,000, projects fiscal revenues near $2.3 billion this year versus $617 million without intervention, and in April announced strategic stockpiles of cobalt, coltan and germanium.
frame_summary: The op-ed argues that Kinshasa is deliberately copying the statecraft playbook of China and the US, using quotas and strategic reserves to turn the DRC from a passive exporter into a price-setting actor in critical minerals.
verbatim_quote: Cobalt prices have risen from approximately $21,000 per tonne in early 2025 to just over $56,000 today.

title: New executive order tightens defense supply chain waiver rules
key_claim: The 20 July executive order requires defence contractors seeking waivers to prove they searched for alternatives, disclose where materials originate and plan to move away from prohibited suppliers, or face loss of contracts, and directs the Pentagon to require mapping of critical defence supply chains from raw materials to finished systems.
frame_summary: Defense News frames the order as the administration's latest move to force contractors off Chinese and other prohibited suppliers, with adviser Peter Navarro casting supply-chain mapping as battlefield preparation rather than paperwork.
verbatim_quote: Contractors will face the loss of contracts if they don’t prove they are doing enough to source domestically.

title: TMC shares soar as NOAA backs seabed mining plan
key_claim: NOAA ruled TMC's consolidated deep-seabed mining application fully compliant on 1 May 2026, advancing the Clarion-Clipperton Zone project toward a potential final permit by early 2027; the application spans about 65,000 sq km, up from roughly 25,000 sq km in its 2025 filing, with an estimated 619 million tonnes of wet nodules.
frame_summary: The report frames the NOAA compliance ruling as a milestone that strengthens TMC's position to open a new source of critical metals, enabled by a January 2026 rule combining exploration and commercial-recovery approval into one process.
verbatim_quote: TMC’s consolidated application spans about 65,000 km², up from roughly 25,000 km² in its 2025 filing, and outlines an estimated 619 million tonnes of wet nodules with additional upside.
